t.E357.agn: In 1977 JECFA set a group acceptable daily intake (ADI) for adipic acid and its potassium, sodium and ammonium salts of 0–5 mg/kg body weight. In 1999 JECFA also evaluated adipic acid as a flavouring substance and found no safety concern at current intake levels. In the EU, the maximum permitted levels for adipic acid and its salts apply together (as adipic acid).
t.E357.body: Adipic acid is largely excreted in the urine without being broken down in the body: in rats, about 70% of an oral dose was found unchanged in the urine. No adipic acid residues were seen in body fats or proteins.
t.E357.found.3: Fillings and toppings of fine bakery wares
t.E357.found.4: Powders for home preparation of drinks (including instant tea and herbal infusion powders)
t.E357.prod: Produced by chemical synthesis from petrochemical raw materials.
t.E357.regx.0: ADI 0–5 mg/kg body weight for adipic acid and its potassium, sodium and ammonium salts.
t.E357.regx.1: Permitted only in certain products (E 355–357 together, as adipic acid): 1,000 mg/kg in powdered dessert mixes and fruit-flavoured desserts, 2,000 mg/kg in fillings and toppings of fine bakery wares, 6,000 mg/kg in gel-like desserts, 10,000 mg/kg in powders for home preparation of drinks.
t.E357.summary: The potassium salt of adipic acid. Used as an acidity regulator.
t.E357.what: The potassium salt of adipic acid, used as an acidity regulator in desserts.
